The S&P 500 has long been a favorite among investors looking to build wealth, with historical annual returns averaging around 10%. But former investment banker Nischa Shah says she’s changing how she invests, and artificial intelligence is a big reason why.

Shah, a qualified accountant and financial educator, recently shared why she’s putting more of her money into global stocks. Her concern isn’t that AI will fail, but that the U.S. stock market has become too dependent on a small group of companies.

Don’t Miss:

  • America Has A Housing Problem. It’s Not Just About Low-Income Housing. A Growing Shortage Is Hitting The Workers Who Keep Communities Running.
  • AI Is Writing More Code Than Ever. Now The Industry Is Running Into A New Problem.

Seven Companies Hold More Weight Than You Think

“When you invest in the S&P 500, your money isn’t split evenly between the 500 companies,” Shah said in a recent video. “In reality, a surprisingly large amount of your investment is divided across just seven companies.”

So, a large portion goes into Apple (NASDAQ:AAPL), Microsoft (NASDAQ:MSFT), Nvidia (NASDAQ:NVDA), Amazon (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet (NASDAQ:GOOG, GOOGL)), Meta (NASDAQ:META) and Tesla (NASDAQ:TSLA), collectively known as the Magnificent Seven.

All seven are investing heavily in AI. While that could result in substantial growth, Shah worries that excitement surrounding the technology may have pushed some company valuations too high.

She compared the situation to the dot-com bubble of the late 1990s, when investors poured money into internet companies, driving stock prices up before the market crashed.

“Even the most successful technology that changes the entire world can still become overhyped in the short term,” she said.

Shah believes AI will transform industries, but that doesn’t mean every company investing in it can justify its current stock price.

Trending: Think Your IRA Can Only Hold Stocks And Funds? Think Again. Here’s What A Self-Directed IRA Can Actually Invest In.

Why She’s Putting More Money Into Global Stocks

Shah isn’t abandoning the S&P 500. Instead, she’s increasing her exposure to companies outside the U.S.

She pointed to Britain and Japan, which dominated global markets at different points in history, as reminders that no country stays on top forever.

“When you only invest in the S&P 500, you miss out on lots of incredibly successful businesses based everywhere else in the world,” she said. To her, these are companies like Samsung Electronics, Toyota (NYSE:TM), Nestlé and AstraZeneca (NASDAQ:AZN).

Shah currently keeps around 80% of her investments in diversified funds and 20% in individual stocks. For beginners, she suggested limiting individual stocks to around 5% or less because of their unpredictable price swings.

And for investors interested in opportunities beyond traditional stocks, entertainment is another industry attracting investment. Skybound Entertainment, the company behind hit shows “The Walking Dead” and “Invincible,” is opening investment opportunities to the public, with shares starting at $12.50.

With a 20-year track record, Skybound reports a $700 million valuation and more than 7,000 shareholders. Investors interested in owning a piece of the company can explore its current share offering.

For Shah, the bigger concern is what happens when investments suddenly lose value. She warned that inexperienced investors sometimes panic and sell after a sharp decline, turning a potentially temporary drop into a permanent loss.

That’s why she’s focused on spreading her money across different countries and industries instead of trying to predict which companies will win.

“The point is you don’t need to know exactly what happens to be a successful investor,” she said. “You just need to build a portfolio that can hopefully perform well across lots of different possible scenarios.”

Building Wealth Across More Than Just The Market

Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That’s why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn’t tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry.

EquityMultiple 

For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and bonds, EquityMultiple provides access to vetted commercial real estate deals starting at $5,000, with only ~5% of opportunities passing their due diligence process. 

Arrived

Backed by Jeff Bezos, Arrived Homes makes real estate investing accessible with a low barrier to entry. Investors can buy fractional shares of single-family rentals and vacation homes starting with as little as $100. This allows everyday investors to diversify into real estate, collect rental income, and build long-term wealth without needing to manage properties directly.

Skybound Entertainment

Entertainment franchises can become valuable long-term assets when they successfully expand across multiple platforms. Skybound Entertainment, the company behind The Walking Dead and Invincible, develops original intellectual property that spans comics, television, film, video games, merchandise, and licensing. With more than 250 IPs in its portfolio and a strategy focused on retaining franchise rights while scaling successful stories across media, Skybound offers investors exposure to the growing entertainment and creator economy through a private company rather than traditional public market investments.

American PowerGen

As artificial intelligence drives a surge in electricity demand, reliable power generation is becoming a critical part of the technology ecosystem. American PowerGen is developing natural gas-fired power plants in Texas, a fast-growing market fueled by AI data centers, manufacturing expansion, and population growth. By advancing projects through permitting, fuel supply, and grid interconnection, the company is positioning itself to help meet rising energy needs while offering investors exposure to the infrastructure supporting the next wave of AI and industrial growth.

Bito

As AI coding tools take on more of the work traditionally done by developers, companies are facing new challenges around code quality, context and the rising cost of AI-powered development. Bito is building software designed to help AI coding agents better understand complex codebases while helping companies control AI development costs. Founded by former PubMatic executives, Bito has raised more than $10 million from institutional and individual investors and is now raising additional capital through a Wefunder offering, giving investors an opportunity to invest in a company targeting an emerging need within the rapidly expanding AI software market.

DLP Capital

For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and traditional real estate opportunities, DLP Capital provides access to private real estate strategies focused on workforce housing — homes for essential workers such as teachers, nurses, firefighters, and police officers. With more than $5.5 billion in assets under management and a community of 4,000+ accredited investors, DLP Capital gives investors access to real estate strategies designed around the growing need for housing that working Americans can actually afford.

FarmTogether

Farmland has historically held its value through market volatility and delivered returns uncorrelated to stocks and bonds. For accredited investors, FarmTogether offers direct access to high-quality U.S. farmland starting at $15,000 — fully managed, with no landlord headaches.

Fundrise

Private real estate and private credit can add income and stability to a stock-heavy portfolio. Fundrise offers access to diversified private real estate and credit strategies through an easy-to-use platform, with professionally managed portfolios designed to generate passive income and long-term growth.

Michael Burry expects the next phase of the stock market to resemble the months after the dot-com peak in 2000, when the biggest winners fell hard and the stocks investors had abandoned climbed.

In an Oct. 17 post on his "Cassandra Unchained" Substack, the investor best known for his bet against the housing market laid out a base case built on four decades of market breadth data.

The market, he wrote, will fail in a way that lifts the median broken stock.

  • PLTR stock is moving. See the real-time price action here.

Burry sees prices drifting lower rather than collapsing in one crash, with some violent stretches along the way, as fundamental news makes its way into the AI narrative.

The AI trade has been a recurring target on his Substack.

In an Oct. 7 post, Burry wrote that the tech giants, other than Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL), are spending as if their lives depended on it. 

The heaviest AI spenders include Microsoft Corp. (NASDAQ:MSFT), Amazon.com Inc. (NASDAQ:AMZN), Alphabet Inc. (NASDAQ:GOOGL) (NASDAQ:GOOG) and Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META). Burry has also published lengthy critiques of Palantir Technologies Inc. (NASDAQ:PLTR).

The March 2000 Template

Burry studied every S&P 500 record close since 1985 that came just before a bear market or a near miss. He split each index into leaders and broken stocks, the latter being names already 20% or more below their 10-year highs when the index peaked.

Only one top produced a clean split. After March 24, 2000, the leaders lost 33% in a year and 50% in 18 months. Two-thirds of them sat more than 20% lower a year after the peak, a share that rose to 79% after 18 months.

The broken stocks went the other way. The median name gained 14% over the first year and held an 8% gain at 18 months. Strength among the laggards pulled the median index member up 5% a year after the top, even as the S&P 500 headed toward a roughly 50% decline over two and a half years.

Burry called the numbers "incredible and unique." No other top in his data saw leaders fall while broken stocks rose at both the 12- and 18-month marks.

Read Also: CoreWeave Stock Down 56% From its Peak — HSBC Sees More Pain Ahead

How Other Tops Played Out

The rest of the record followed different scripts. In 1987 and 2022, everything fell, with leaders doing slightly worse. In 1990, 2007, 2011, 2015 and 2018, broken stocks fell further over the following year as weakness spread outward from the weakest names.

The 2020 and 2025 sell-offs took both groups down together. Both were higher a year later.

Burry noted one partial echo. During the DeepSeek scare in early 2025, which hit AI leaders such as NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA), broken stocks outperformed the leaders before April’s tariff shock dragged everything down.

See More: Top Growth Stocks

Why Today Looks Like 2000

Burry’s case rests on breadth. When the S&P 500 closed at a record on Oct. 6, 55% of its members sat at least 20% below their 10-year highs. Among the tops he studied, only March 2000 ranked higher, at 71%. Ordinary tops ran between 20% and 31%.

Just 15 stocks closed at new highs with the index that day, and 97 were within 10% of one. In March 2000, the figures were 15 and 87.

He also flagged a structural difference. A constant mechanical bid from passive and systematic money has kept the deepest losers from piling up the way they did in 2000, he argued. Burry expects that bid to lose steam over the next two years.

Burry describes the bid as pushing more dollars toward fewer of the largest companies in market-cap-weighted indices. 

A rotation like the one he expects would show up in the gap between the cap-weighted SPDR S&P 500 ETF Trust (NYSE:SPY) and the Invesco S&P 500 Equal Weight ETF (NYSE:RSP), which gives every member the same weight.

Timing Remains Open

Burry cautioned the setup typically takes six to nine months to play out. Nobody knows where the clock stands, he wrote, and the market could be at the start, several months in or close to the end.

The bigger worry comes afterward. Burry questioned what could lift stocks again, given a federal government he sees as too stretched to support a private debt bubble when it bursts.

He describes the market as stuck in denial, the first stage of grief. "Denial is a hell of a drug," Burry wrote, "and I will be watching."

Trading in Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) is quiet on Tuesday. Shares have lost more than 10% in just two weeks. They are getting close to support. This could put a floor under the price. This is why NVIDIA is the Stock of the Day.

As you can see on the chart below, the $210 level has been important for NVIDIA. It was resistance in both June and July.

People who bought shares around $210 in June regretted it when the price dropped. Some vowed to exit at breakeven if they could.

When the shares rallied back to $210 in July, they placed sell orders. These orders created resistance.

The $210 level became support in August. This was the result of sellers who regretted their decision.

Some of the people who sold around $210 regretted it when the resistance broke and price moved higher. Some decided to buy their shares back if they could do so at their selling price.

When NVIDIA fell back to $210 in August, they placed buy orders. These orders formed support.

When the stock rallied, many people who sold around $210 decided that was a mistake. They also decided to repurchase their shares at their selling price if possible.

When NVIDIA dropped back to $210 in September, they placed buy orders. These orders created support

If shares reach $210 again, something similar may happen. People who sold in September may try to buy their shares back. This could be where the selloff ends.

NVIDIA may even reverse and rally, as it did the last two times it reached this key level.

Meta Platforms Inc. (NASDAQ:META) is drawing bullish analyst views ahead of its third-quarter earnings report Wednesday, as Wall Street sees growing opportunities in artificial intelligence, advertising and the company’s new Muse AI agent.

The company is scheduled to release its third-quarter 2026 financial results after the market closes on Oct. 21.

Analysts expect earnings of $5.89 per share, down from $7.25 a year earlier. Revenue is projected to rise to $63.36 billion from $51.24 billion in the year-ago quarter.

Ahead of Meta’s earnings report, Rosenblatt Securities and Citizens JMP Securities maintained bullish ratings on the company, with price forecasts of $886 and $885, respectively.

Rosenblatt Sees Strong Advertising Growth Ahead

Rosenblatt analyst Barton Crockett maintained a Buy rating and an $886 price forecast, citing Meta’s advertising momentum and potential AI-driven growth.

Crockett said Meta’s decision to report earnings a week earlier than usual, without issuing preliminary results, suggests management is confident about its performance.

He expects third-quarter revenue growth near the upper end of Meta’s 19% to 25% guidance range, supported by AI-driven improvements in advertising engagement and effectiveness.

Rosenblatt projects third-quarter revenue of $63.94 billion, above the $63.36 billion consensus estimate. Adjusted earnings are expected to reach $6.95 per share, according to the firm’s estimates.

However, Crockett expects Meta’s substantial AI investments to pressure free cash flow. He sees capital spending of $130 billion to $145 billion in 2026 and considers a potential increase toward $200 billion in 2027 reasonable.

Despite those costs, Crockett believes Meta’s core advertising improvements can justify its AI investments, with Muse providing additional long-term upside.

Space Exploration Technologies Corp. (NASDAQ) heads into third-quarter earnings with investors focused on Starship progress, Starlink’s wireless ambitions, AI infrastructure spending and whether the company can deliver on its aggressive long-term revenue goals.

Consensus estimates call for third-quarter revenue of $12.74 billion and EPS of 14 cents.

• What’s ahead for SPCX stock?

Bank of America Says Starship and Revenue Targets Matter Most

Bank of America Securities senior aerospace analyst Ron Epstein said the most important earnings discussion will center on SpaceX’s larger financial and operational targets.

Management previously outlined a goal of reaching roughly a $100 billion revenue run rate by year-end and about $1 trillion by 2030. Epstein told CNBC on Tuesday that Bank of America’s projections reach the trillion-dollar mark roughly one to two years later.

He also called Starship central to SpaceX’s future because it supports Starlink expansion, orbital computing and other businesses. Epstein expects investors to watch for updates on the heat shield, future launches, possible Starship and Super Heavy catches and performance of the new Starlink V3 satellites, which he said deliver about 10 times the throughput of V2 satellites.

Analysts Debate Starlink Mobile Economics

Epstein said SpaceX’s low-band spectrum purchases strengthen its ability to pursue mobile services, while its more than 10,000 Starlink satellites give it a global network advantage.

MoffettNathanson analyst Julie Zhu questioned whether Starlink can economically compete with AT&T Inc. (NYSE:T), T-Mobile US Inc. (NASDAQ:TMUS) and Verizon Communications Inc. (NYSE:VZ). She said terrestrial carriers still control substantially more spectrum and warned that building comparable coverage would require significant capital.

Bernstein analyst Madison Rezaei sees another path, arguing that SpaceX could partner with existing carriers and become an additional tenant for U.S. tower operators, potentially increasing recurring tower revenue by roughly 10%-15%.

Wall Street Sees More Growth from AI and Connectivity

Goldman Sachs reiterated a Buy rating and raised its SpaceX price forecast to $230 from $220.

Jim Cramer also remains bullish on the underlying business, citing Starlink cash flow, reusable rockets and expanding AI-compute capacity. "I really like SpaceX, the company, because I believe it’ll become much more profitable as cash flows from Starlink take off," Cramer said.

SpaceX is reportedly seeking another $40 billion to acquire more NVIDIA Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) chips and expand computing capacity. Cramer said the company can monetize that hardware by renting excess compute to outside customers.

Still, valuation remains a key debate. Cramer noted that SpaceX trades at roughly 137 times next-12-month earnings, underscoring the need for execution across Starlink, AI and Starship to support investor expectations.

Danny Moses, who helped bet against the housing bubble before the 2008 financial crisis, has compared CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) to WeWork, questioning whether the AI cloud provider can turn a profit while carrying enormous financial obligations.

“It’s really like a WeWork,” Moses said on Monday’s episode of The Real Eisman Playbook, hosted by his former colleague Steve Eisman.

Moses cited roughly $51 billion in debt and lease obligations, prompting Eisman to call the figure “frightening.”

The WeWork Problem

Moses said CoreWeave has begun renting computing capacity on shorter terms, potentially creating a mismatch with its long-term debts and leases.

That resembles WeWork’s model of signing long-term office leases while relying on shorter-term rentals to cover its costs.

CoreWeave’s June filing showed approximately $35.1 billion in debt and $16.5 billion in lease liabilities. Its operating leases had an average of 12 years remaining, while the GPUs powering its business face rapid technological change.

Echoes of 2000 and 2008

Moses recalled the dot-com boom, when telecom companies spent billions laying fiber-optic networks in anticipation of soaring internet demand.

“They were right. They were right,” he said of investors who believed the internet would transform the world.

But the spending exceeded what the economics could support.

“The math didn’t work,” Moses said.

He also drew parallels with 2008, when Wall Street financed mortgage lenders and packaged their loans into securities for investors.

Moses pointed to a partnership between Nvidia Corp. (NASDAQ:NVDA) and Wall Street banks to securitize AI infrastructure financing, saying such deals are already starting.

BlackRock Inc. (NYSE:BLK) CEO Larry Fink compared the initiative to the early mortgage-backed securities market, prompting an incredulous reaction from Moses.

“What did you just say?” he recalled thinking.

Wall Street Divided on CoreWeave

CoreWeave’s 2031 bonds yielded 15.58% Tuesday, reflecting mounting concern over its ability to service its debt.

JPMorgan expects CoreWeave’s free cash flow to remain negative until 2030, although it considers banks’ exposures relatively well secured.

Yet Goldman Sachs upgraded the stock to Buy on Monday, arguing investors overestimate its future financing costs.

CoreWeave also reported $103.7 billion in remaining performance obligations at the end of June, representing contracted revenue, not guaranteed profits.

On Polymarket, traders put the chance of CoreWeave announcing bankruptcy by the end of 2027 at 10%, rising to 29% by the end of 2029.

Moses stopped short of predicting bankruptcy, acknowledging he hadn’t analyzed the company closely enough to judge its eventual profitability.

“That’s not a stock I want to own to express my AI theme,” he said.

On Tuesday, Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META) said it has suspended the Muse AI conversation-sharing feature after security researchers found that public domain name system (DNS) records could expose thousands of shared chat links.

Researchers Uncover 6,800 Muse AI Chat Links

Over the weekend, security researchers at Claroc found that Muse generated sharing URLs using a predictable format, incorporating conversation titles into web addresses under a common domain structure.

According to Claroc, this made the links discoverable through passive DNS searches, which use archived records of domain name system activity to identify internet addresses.

"Muse names each share’s web address after the conversation’s own title, and that address is written into public DNS," Claroc said in a blog post. "One passive-DNS search brings back thousands of them, listed by name, like a table of contents."

Claroc said it identified approximately 6,800 shared Muse chat links and accessed conversations containing sensitive information.

The material included meeting details involving a leading AI lab, a small-business loan application, a bank fraud alert with partial account information, a company’s vacation calendar and internal business documents.

Read Also: Meta Heads Into Earnings With AI Ambitions Soaring, Cash Burn in Focus

Meta Pauses Muse AI Sharing Feature

Ars Technica first reported on Claroc’s findings.

In a statement emailed to Benzinga on Tuesday, a Meta spokesperson said the company launched the Muse bug bounty program to let researchers identify potential issues and help improve the product, adding that shared Muse content generates a webpage accessible to anyone with the link.

“However, we’ve paused this functionality while we review this report and consider changes to how these links can be discovered,” the Meta spokesperson stated.

Claroc subsequently reported that researchers could no longer open a sample of links they had previously accessed following Meta’s update. "We are glad to see it closed this quickly," the update read.

Meta’s Muse AI Faces Privacy Concerns Ahead of Earnings

In September, technology columnist Jason Aten of Inc. magazine alleged that Meta’s Muse accessed private messages on his Mac despite him never enabling the "Full Disk Access" permission.

At the time, Meta spokesperson Andy Stone rejected the allegation, saying Muse can access Apple Inc.’s (NASDAQ:AAPL) Messages app only when users explicitly opt in. This might also interest you.

Meta will report its third-quarter results after the market closes on Wednesday. Analysts expect revenue of $63.36 billion, up from $51.24 billion a year earlier. The company has beaten revenue estimates for more than 10 consecutive quarters.

Tech analyst Dan Ives expects Meta to monetize its 3.5 billion-user base through its Muse AI agent, which he says could make AI more accessible through Facebook and Instagram.

Truist, according to market strategist Shay Boloor, projects that Muse will generate approximately $29 billion in revenue by 2030, including an estimated $11 billion from subscriptions.

On Tuesday, Futurum Equities chief market strategist Shay Boloor highlighted comments from Elon Musk during Space Exploration Technologies Corp.’s (NASDAQ:SPCX) third-quarter earnings call, raising questions about whether the industry has enough infrastructure to meet surging demand.

SpaceX Struggles to Find Available Chips

During the earnings call, Musk stated that he expects the shortage of superintelligence computing capacity to persist for years, adding that SpaceX’s short-term compute contracts are renewing at higher prices.

"We are also frankly hounded relentlessly by every hyperscaler and by dozens of smaller companies to rent more of our compute. So we could rent out our compute several times over if we said yes to everyone," the SpaceX CEO said.

Musk also said SpaceX tried to shift some inference workloads to other cloud providers to free up capacity for AI training but struggled to find available Nvidia Corp.’s (NASDAQ:NVDA) GB300 and GB200 systems, Alphabet Inc.’s (NASDAQ:GOOG) (NASDAQ:GOOGL) Google TPUs, Amazon.com, Inc.’s (NASDAQ:AMZN) Trainium chips and Nvidia H100 GPUs.

"So I don’t think we’re going to have a demand issue here. And like, it’s not impossible—I’m not saying this will happen—it’s not impossible that we will have a six month payback period for compute next year," the tech mogul said.

Read Also: SpaceX, Netflix, Super Micro Computer, Tesla and Meta: Why These 5 Stocks Are on Investors' Radars Today

Strategist Says AI Chip Shortage Is Far From Over

"That’s pretty insane coming from one of world’s largest AI infrastructure builders because the shortage extends across nearly every major chip architecture," Boloor wrote on X.

He added, "And if SpaceX can’t find spare capacity despite its scale and willingness to pay then it’s getting much harder to argue we’re already in a broad AI compute glut."

SpaceX Reports Strong AI Revenue Growth

SpaceX reported third-quarter revenue of $14.58 billion, beating analyst estimates of $12.74 billion. Earnings came in at 35 cents per share, compared with expectations of 12 cents.

Revenue climbed 161% year over year, led by its Super Intelligence business, which generated $7.6 billion, up 830%. Connectivity revenue, including Starlink, rose 69% to $5.2 billion, while the space business grew 6% to $1.8 billion.

SpaceX said its third-quarter capital expenditures totaled $19.6 billion, primarily driven by investments in its superintelligence computing infrastructure, Starship infrastructure and satellite production.

CoreWeave Inc. (NASDAQ:CRWV) stock rose in Wednesday’s premarket trading as Wall Street analysts remained divided over the AI cloud provider’s growth prospects and mounting debt.

Bulls point to CoreWeave’s limited AI-computing capacity, long-term customer contracts and expanding infrastructure. However, bears warn that rising borrowing costs, heavy debt and competition from major cloud providers could pressure profitability.

Nasdaq futures gained 0.41%, while S&P 500 futures rose 0.07%.

Compass Point Highlights CoreWeave’s AI Capacity Advantage

Compass Point senior analyst Michael Donovan remains bullish on CoreWeave, citing its secured power capacity and expanding technology offerings.

Donovan told CNBC on Monday that CoreWeave had about 1.85 gigawatts of powered capacity at the end of the second quarter. He expects the company to secure roughly 3 gigawatts by the end of 2027.

He identified limited AI-computing capacity as a major industry bottleneck.

Donovan also defended CoreWeave’s financing model. The company borrows against customer contracts that typically run three to five years.

Under this structure, GPUs backed by five-year agreements could become fully paid for around the third year. That would allow them to generate additional cash to meet corporate obligations.

He described the business as “complex, but not complicated,” emphasizing execution and longer GPU useful lives.

See More: Top Value Stocks

HSBC Warns of Lower Margins and Competitive Pressure

HSBC maintained its Reduce rating and $39 price forecast, citing structural disadvantages compared with major cloud providers.

The bank expects CoreWeave to generate about $12 million in annual revenue per megawatt in 2027. That compares with $17 million to $18 million for hyperscalers.

According to HSBC, major cloud providers benefit from diversified businesses and more profitable short-term customers. Meanwhile, neocloud operators depend heavily on large clients renting relatively standardized GPU capacity.

HSBC’s adjusted earnings estimates for 2028 through 2030 remain 50% to 70% below Wall Street consensus. The firm also expects long-term operating margins of 15% to 16%, well below management’s roughly 25% target.

Evercore and Goldman Sachs Defend CoreWeave’s Debt Strategy

Evercore ISI analyst Amit Daryanani maintained an Outperform rating and $150 price forecast.

Daryanani said much of CoreWeave’s financing is backed by contracts with Meta Platforms, Inc. (NASDAQ:META), Microsoft Corporation (NASDAQ:MSFT) and OpenAI, carrying borrowing costs of around 5.5%.

However, he argued that investors are placing too much emphasis on unsecured debt yielding 14% to 15%.

Evercore estimates project-level returns on invested capital of 15% to 20%. The firm believes CoreWeave could absorb a 100- to 200-basis-point increase in borrowing costs without significantly weakening project economics.

Meanwhile, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges upgraded CoreWeave to Buy from Neutral. However, she lowered her price forecast to $106 from $139.

Borges argued that investors may be overstating CoreWeave’s future borrowing costs while overlooking stronger project returns and recent increases in computing prices.

Credit Markets Could Determine CoreWeave’s Next Move

Despite analysts’ bullish arguments, financing remains a major concern.

Great Hill Capital Chairman Thomas Hayes warned that skepticism in the bond market could keep CoreWeave’s borrowing costs elevated.

Shorecliff Asset Management’s Grant Nachman cautioned that large unsecured financing deals could become prohibitively expensive for neocloud operators.

Meanwhile, MetLife Investment Management’s John Yovanovic highlighted the substantial supply of AI-related debt expected to enter credit markets over the next 18 months.

The contrasting views underscore a central question for investors: Can CoreWeave turn surging AI infrastructure demand into sustainable profits before financing costs erode its returns?
